title: Steps to Help
why: People write step-by-step instructions so that someone else can do a task.

title: Steps for a Kind Act
why: A good set of steps starts from thinking about the person who will follow it.

title: Who Helped My Morning?
why: A daily routine written as steps shows how many people help at each one.

title: Fair Steps for Everyone
why: A fair algorithm gives every person the same steps, so writing one for sharing out materials makes fairness something you can check.

title: Fix the Recipe
why: Algorithms rarely work the first time, so testing a set of steps and revising them shows that trying again is part of the process.

title: Whose Steps Are Better?
why: Asking whether there is a shorter way to do the same job is where algorithm thinking begins.

title: Write It Together
why: A shared set of steps only works if everyone agrees on what each step means, which takes talking and listening.

title: Follow It Exactly
why: To test an algorithm you must follow the steps exactly as written and report what really happened, even if it fails.

title: Order the Helping Steps
why: Helping well often depends on doing things in the right order, such as asking before you act, so sequencing makes that visible.

title: What Comes First for a Friend?
why: Caring for someone has an order too: notice first, then ask, then help. Putting those steps in order practises reading a situation.

title: Thank-You in Order
why: A good thank-you has steps, such as noticing, saying it and showing it, and ordering them shows what gratitude involves.

title: My Turn Your Turn
why: Building a sequence one block at a time gives each person an equal share of the making.

title: Fix the Order
why: When the order is wrong the program fails, and putting it right takes another try.

title: What If We Swap Two Steps?
why: Changing the order and seeing what happens is a direct way to ask what if.

title: Human Robot
why: Giving and following instructions in order needs two people working closely.

title: The True Order
why: Reporting the real order in which things happened, not the order we wish they had, is a small exercise in truthful telling.

title: Keep Helping Loop
why: Helping is often repeated, like handing out papers each day, and a loop shows how a small repeated act adds up.

title: Kind Words on Repeat
why: A loop can repeat a kind act, and asking when to stop repeating it brings in noticing how the other person feels.

title: Thank-You on Repeat
why: Some good actions are worth repeating every day.

title: Everyone Gets a Turn Loop
why: A loop that visits every person once is a simple model of giving everyone a turn.

title: The Cat That Kept Trying
why: A loop repeats the same small effort until the goal is reached.

title: How Many Times?
why: Changing how many times a loop repeats and watching the result is an easy way to ask what if.

title: Our Dance Loop
why: A repeating pattern made by two people only works if they keep in step.

title: Count It Truly
why: Counting how many times a loop really ran, not how many we meant, practises reporting what actually happened.

title: Tap to Help
why: A character can be programmed to respond when someone needs it.

title: Bump Then Be Kind
why: What happens after a bump is a choice, in a program and in real life.

title: Thank-You Button
why: An event can trigger a response, so a button that plays a thank-you shows how noticing help leads to saying thanks.

title: Same Event Same Response
why: Programs respond the same way to the same event for everyone, which is a simple picture of treating people alike.

title: Try the Button Again
why: Events do not always do what we expect, so testing and trying again until the right event fires builds patience.

title: What Will It Do?
why: An event block invites the question of what will set the program going.

title: You Send I Respond
why: One part of a program sends an event and another responds, like teammates who each wait for the other's signal.

title: Does It Really Respond?
why: Checking that the event really fires, and saying so when it does not, is honest testing.

title: If Someone Needs Help Then...
why: Noticing a need is the if, and helping is the then, which makes service a rule you can build.

title: If a Friend Is Sad Then...
why: Noticing how someone feels is the 'if' that leads to a kind 'then'.

title: If Someone Helped Then Thank
why: A rule that says if someone helped me then I thank them turns gratitude into a habit you can write down.

title: If Someone Has Not Had a Turn
why: An if-then rule applies the same way to everyone, which is what makes it fair.

title: If It Fails Then Try Again
why: A rule that says if the first try fails then try another way is a simple model of not giving up.

title: What If the Answer Changes?
why: Changing the condition and seeing a different result is a hands-on way to ask what if.

title: If We Disagree Then...
why: Writing a rule for what the group does when members disagree makes teamwork's hard moments planned.

title: If I Made a Mistake Then I Say So
why: A true answer to the 'if' question is needed for the rule to work.

title: Count Our Helping
why: A variable can keep count of how many times we helped, which makes small acts of service visible.

title: Feelings Meter
why: Storing a feeling in a variable lets a program respond to it, which practises noticing how others feel.

title: Thank-You Counter
why: Keeping a count of thank-yous given or received makes gratitude something we can notice and grow.

title: The Turn Counter
why: A value that stores whose turn it is helps everyone share fairly.

title: Try Counter
why: A variable that counts attempts shows that many tries are normal and progress is real.

title: What If I Change the Number?
why: Changing a stored value and watching what happens invites the question 'what if?'.

title: Team Score
why: A single shared variable that everyone adds to shows how individual efforts become one result.

title: Keep the Real Score
why: A stored value is only useful if it is the real one.

title: Bug Helpers
why: Helping a classmate find a bug without taking over their keyboard is practice in useful, respectful help.

title: Kind Bug Buddies
why: A classmate whose program fails needs encouragement before advice.

title: Thank the Bug Finder
why: When someone finds a bug in our work they are helping us, and saying thank you instead of feeling embarrassed changes how mistakes feel.

title: Fair Bug Blame
why: Bugs are not anyone's fault, and discussing where a bug really came from avoids unfair blame.

title: Bug Hunt Try Again
why: Finding the step that fails and fixing it means trying again with a plan.

title: Be a Bug Detective
why: Treating a bug as a mystery to investigate rather than a failure builds curiosity about how the program really works.

title: Two Heads Find Bugs
why: Two people often find a bug faster than one, because each notices what the other misses.

title: I Found My Bug
why: Fixing a bug starts with saying plainly what went wrong.

title: Test It for Someone Else
why: Testing a program for the person who will use it is a way of serving them.

title: Test With Kindness
why: Testers can say what is wrong without hurting the maker, which practises kind and honest feedback.

title: Thank Your Testers
why: Testers give their time to improve our work, and thanking them acknowledges the effort.

title: Test for Everyone
why: A good test checks that a program works for different kinds of users, not only the easiest case.

title: Test It Again
why: One test is rarely enough, so testing means coming back to it.

title: Predict Run Change
why: A test is a way of finding out something you do not know yet.

title: Test Each Other's Work
why: Swapping programs to test each other's work builds trust that feedback is meant to help.

title: Say What Really Happened
why: Testing only works if you report what actually happened.

title: Break Up a Big Helping Job
why: A big helping job like tidying the classroom becomes doable when split into small parts, which makes service feel possible.

title: Understand the Whole Person
why: Breaking a problem into parts is like noticing the different things a person may be feeling instead of putting one big label on it.

title: Many Parts Many Helpers
why: Big things are made of many parts, each done by someone.

title: Fair Shares of the Job
why: Splitting a job into parts raises the question of who does which part, which is a question about fairness.

title: One Small Part at a Time
why: A big job feels possible when it is done one small part at a time.

title: What Are the Parts?
why: Taking something apart to see what it is made of is a way of asking how it works.

title: Split the Job
why: Once a job is split into parts, each person can take one.

title: Say What Is Done
why: When a job is in parts, each person must say honestly whether their part is finished.

title: Notice a Need Pattern
why: Noticing a pattern, such as the same job always left undone, shows where help is most needed.

title: Pattern of Feelings
why: Noticing when a friend is often sad at the same time or place is a pattern that points to how to care.

title: Patterns of Kindness
why: Looking for the pattern of who helps us each day shows how much we usually overlook.

title: Does the Rule Fit Everyone?
why: A sorting rule can leave something out, and a fair rule has a place for everything.

title: Pattern Puzzle Persist
why: Finding a pattern can take several wrong guesses, and keeping going after each one is the skill.

title: Pattern Detectives
why: Finding a pattern begins with noticing what is the same and what is different.

title: Pattern Pairs
why: Two people can often spot a pattern one would miss and test it together.

title: Say What You See
why: A pattern is only useful if we describe what we really see.

title: Helper Hands
why: Helping a partner well means leaving them able to do it themselves.

title: Kind Partners
why: Working closely with a partner means noticing when they are frustrated and responding kindly.

title: Thank Your Partner
why: Pairs depend on each other, and thanking a partner for what they contributed builds appreciation.

title: Fair Shares of the Keyboard
why: A shared device needs fair turns.

title: Stuck Together
why: When two people get stuck together they can encourage each other to try again.

title: Ask Your Partner Why
why: Asking a partner why they chose something teaches both people to explain and wonder.

title: Driver and Navigator
why: Two programmers on one project succeed only by planning and working together.

title: Say What You Think
why: Good partners say honestly when an idea is not working, kindly and clearly.

title: A Project for Someone
why: A project can be made for someone else's enjoyment.

title: One Kind True Thing
why: Looking at a classmate's work is a chance to find the good in it and say so.

title: Thank-You Credits
why: Finishing a project is the moment to thank the people who helped.

title: Fair Showcase
why: Sharing projects raises the question of whether everyone gets a fair chance to show their work.

title: Show the Messy Middle
why: Showing the tries and fixes behind a finished project celebrates persistence.

title: Questions for the Maker
why: Asking a classmate genuine questions about their project shows interest in how it was made.

title: Showcase Together
why: A shared showcase needs everyone to agree on how to present the group's work.

title: What Is Really Mine?
why: Presenting a project honestly means saying what we did ourselves and what we had help with.
